title: Poland vs Turkey vs Australia vs Romania vs New Zealand – white bollard with a red reflector
intro: All are plain white posts with a red reflector on the front. The difference is what the red does: wraps around, stays on the front only, or stops halfway – and what is on the back.

items.note: Red strip wraps all the way around; red reflector front, white reflector on the back. Often a number on it. Also a thinner curved version. (Same design only in Zakarpattia, Ukraine.)
Rectangular, flat (thin from the side), red reflector only on the front, nothing on the back. Rare yellow version in snowy areas.
Red reflector on the front that stops in the middle of the post, grey reflector on the back. If unsure: sun position, landscape, vegetation.
Thin white post with a red vertical strip near the top – looks like Turkey, but bollards are rare in Romania.
Like Australia but the red reflector wraps around to the back (goes end to end) instead of stopping in the middle.

tip: Back of the bollard: white = Poland, grey = Australia, red continuing = NZ, nothing = Turkey/Romania.

title: Austria vs Slovenia vs Montenegro vs Serbia vs Germany vs Switzerland – black top, grey/red reflector
intro: Central-European family: white wedge, black top, small reflector. Reflector colour and position decide.

items.note: White, black top, reflector dark red or dark grey; often a small nipple-shaped black cap and sometimes a snow pole on top.
Same shape as Austria but reflector is bright red on the front and white on the back (Austria: dark/grey back).
Very similar to Slovenia: red front, white back. Decide by landscape/language (Cyrillic/Latin mix, ‑ić names).
Several designs but reflector is always off-centre; bollards are flat with no depth.
Black-and-white with white / light-grey reflectors (orange at intersections), often road-number plates and blue side attachments; one every ~50 m.
Black-and-white, white or grey reflectors; wedge-shaped or cylindrical with a rounded top. Liechtenstein uses the same round ones.

tip: Bright red front + white back → Slovenia/Montenegro. Dark red/grey → Austria. Grey only → Germany/Switzerland. Off-centre → Serbia.

title: Czechia vs Slovakia – identical bollards, so look elsewhere
intro: Both use orange double reflectors on the front and one white on the back, the same wide type‑B guardrails, paired round concrete poles and red/white temporary sign posts. Split them with signs:

items.note: Arrow-shaped directional signs with a filled tip; sign borders are separated from the edge; thick black sign-post caps; bright red street signs.
Blue directional signs with small white arrows; borders usually on the edge; white street signs with blue text and thin red border; word ulica; small signs often on double posts; more wooden poles.

tip: Street name with “ulica” = Slovakia (never in Czechia).

title: Hungary vs Croatia vs Bulgaria vs Lithuania – wedge with a black band
intro: Generic ‘wedge + reflector’ bollards. Hungary and Croatia are the real 50/50.

items.note: Black-and-white wedge, red front reflector, white back; blue reflectors also common. More rounded edges; reflector sits a bit lower than Croatia.
White with a black rectangle, red or white reflector; triangular from the top, sharper edges; the reflector is closer to the top and bollards look thinner.
Similar generic design but bollards are fairly rare; red front, white back; inconsistent shapes.
Wedge-shaped with orange rectangular front reflector and white rectangular back reflector.

tip: Orange reflector → Lithuania. Rounded + low reflector → Hungary. Sharp + high reflector → Croatia.

title: Nordics & Baltics – black-and-white bollards
intro: Plonkit's own infographic sums it up; below are the single-country pictures.

items.note: Finland (plonkit's Nordic/Baltic bollard infographic is on the Finland page): long black-and-white, white rectangular front reflector, two dots on the back, black strip diagonal; round or thin-curved.
Black-and-white, usually grey reflector (orange at intersections); wedge, round or thin-curved. Black strip is straight on the baton type.
Thin, curved rectangle; silver reflector inside a black parallelogram; narrow and flat.
Round, baton-like; rectangular front reflector, two circular back reflectors (white or orange).
Thin, slightly curved; rectangular front, two circular back reflectors; black strip slightly angled; often numbered.
Unique: white with a yellow reflector and dark orange stripe (green variant exists).
Unique yellow bollards with a white reflector, everywhere on rural roads.

tip: Yellow → Iceland. Orange stripe → Denmark. Parallelogram → Norway. Baton round → Estonia; thin curved → Latvia; wedge+orange → Lithuania.

title: Denmark vs Belgium vs Netherlands

items.note: Yellow reflector + dark orange stripe at the top.
White with a yellow rectangular reflector on the front, white on the back; never an orange stripe. Second type: dark brown with two red stripes (also NL).
Simple white (or black) bollard with a red reflector. Rare French-style round ones whose red band does not go all the way round.

title: France vs Scotland (UK) – round post with a band

items.note: Round white post with a pointed top and a grey or red band all the way around. Also: round bollard with two indented bands (unique), and wedge with wide white reflectors.
Standard UK: rounded, red front / white back, black base and top, white stripe. Scottish red-and-white round bollard looks French but has a blunt top.

title: Italy vs Albania · Greece vs Andorra

items.note: Triangular, white with black top, red front / white back. Albania uses the same bollard – decide by language, plates, poles.
Same as Italy. Albania: much poorer roads, Albanian language (ë, ç), red plates strip AL.
Wedge with almost square reflectors, red front / white back.
Similar wedge to Greece (and to Spain near the border) but mountainous Pyrenees landscape, Catalan.

title: Spain vs Portugal vs Chile – yellow-orange reflector

items.note: Yellow-orange reflector on the front, two white dots on the back (or blank), typically hollow. Extremadura: green tops; Aragón: flat stick with grey reflectors.
Wedge with a noticeably thin white top, or flat with a wide reflector; mostly white reflectors, sometimes darker orange. Guardrails: red reflectors (Spain: yellow).
Spanish-style but white front / yellow-orange back; not common. Orange temporary bollard with two white stripes.

title: Chevron colours in Europe
intro: Chevrons are one of the quickest splits. Learn the colour families:

items.note: Bulgaria: red on white (same as Romania, Turkey, N. Macedonia). Plonkit has a full European chevron infographic on the Bulgaria page.
White with red arrows: Poland, Lithuania (red outline on singles), Latvia, Belgium, Netherlands, Bulgaria, Romania, Turkey, N. Macedonia, Hungary…
Red with white arrows: Estonia, Russia, Ukraine.
Black with white arrows: Italy, Greece, Albania, UK; Spain too but almost always 2 or 4 arrows.
Spain: black/white or blue/white; France is the only other country with blue/white. Portugal: black with yellow arrows.
Black with yellow arrows: Finland, Norway, Iceland. Sweden: unique blue and yellow.
Black arrow on white: Serbia, Slovenia (also red on white), Montenegro, N. Macedonia.

title: Chevrons in the Americas

items.note: Yellow base, black arrows – like most of Latin America.
Argentina uniquely uses white with red arrows.
Yellow with black arrows – mainly useful against Argentina.
“Chevron spam” in curves – far more chevrons than neighbours (Colombia occasionally too).

title: Pedestrian crossing signs – stripes and belts

items.note: 5 stripes, person with a belt sitting noticeably low (“sagging pants”) – unique to Hungary.
5 stripes, belt at normal height. Slovenia's person has no belt.
5 stripes with belt (same as Germany), or stripes very close together.
5 stripes, simply drawn person, no belt. Austria: two dotted lines instead of stripes.
No stripes, two horizontal dotted lines, square-headed man. France/NL: regular zebra with 5 stripes.
3 stripes, detailed person (shoes, attached head). Lithuania/Russia/Ukraine also 3 stripes but simpler person; Russia often yellow border. Latvia: 5 stripes.
Finland 5 stripes; Sweden and Norway usually 4.

title: Stop signs: Spain vs Portugal · ALTO vs PARE

items.note: Small, compact font. Red borders go to the edge (no white rim), flat sign posts.
Noticeably larger font; thin white rim on red-bordered signs.
ALTO: Mexico, Guatemala, Panama, Costa Rica. PARE: all of South America and Puerto Rico.

title: Guardrails that split neighbours

items.note: Black-and-yellow stripes with a black outer stripe. Bolivia: same but yellow outer stripe. Peru also uses zebra sign posts, Bolivia bulky white square posts.
Yellow/red rectangular reflectors – also in Uruguay. Argentine supports are 3 sides of a rectangle; Uruguay adds bits of the 4th side at the corners.

Plonkit has a European guardrail infographic on the Czechia page. CZ/SK: extra-wide type B. Poland: square B with round red reflectors. Lithuania: A with orange, Latvia red/white, Estonia none, Portugal red, Spain yellow, Norway wooden posts.

title: Nordic road lines

items.note: All white. Small roads: short dashed outer lines; highways: outer line split into small sections.
Yellow middle lines with an orange tinge; small roads have long dashed white outer lines.
Outer lines always solid white (no dashes, except Åland); middle: white dashes, or yellow (being phased out).

title: Chile vs Argentina vs Bolivia vs Uruguay

items.note: Either all white or all yellow (parks/snow) – almost never mixed.
Middle lines yellow, yellow+white, or white; outer always white. Mixed combos common (unlike Chile).
Yellow-white also in Argentina; Argentina also has a lot of all-white roads. Uruguay: smudgy camera, plain white plates.

title: USA vs Canada

items.note: Yellow middle (double most common) + white outer. “SPEED LIMIT”, wordy signs, rectangular junction signs, miles/feet, American spelling; Gen 2 rare (except Alaska).
“MAXIMUM” on speed signs, km/h, British spelling, diamond junction signs, blank railway crossings; more Gen 2/3 coverage; double middle lines less common.

title: Cyrillic: Ukraine vs Russia · Baltic alphabets

items.note: Unique: Є є, Ґ ґ, І і, Ї ї. Plates: blue-yellow strip (Russia: plain white). Chevrons red/white in both.
Ы, Э, Ё, Ъ. Square concrete poles in both; Russian pedestrian signs often yellow-bordered.
Ą Ę Į Ų, Ė, Y; street = gatvė (g.).
Macrons Ā Ē Ī Ū, hooks Ģ Ķ Ļ Ņ; street = iela.
Ä Ö Ü Õ, looks like Finnish (double vowels); street = tee/tänav.

title: Pole families that are easy to mix

items.note: Square concrete poles = post-Soviet (Ukraine, Russia, Lithuania, Estonia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan).
Wide round concrete poles in pairs = Czechia/Slovakia. Upside-down triangle pole-top support also in DE, AL, RS, RO.
Concrete ladder poles with tall steps = Portugal; Spain and France have ladder poles with short steps.
Wooden pole with a small black metal cap = Nordics (+ Estonia, sometimes Latvia). Lamp mount: Sweden double bolt below top, Finland double bolt at top & straight, Norway thick single bolt.
North America: wooden poles, large metal cylinder transformers (never in Europe), insulator raised on top of the pole.
Belgium: square concrete with tiny holes and small metal wrappings (also France); Netherlands has basically no street-level poles.

title: Licence-plate 50/50s

items.note: Plain white, black characters. Argentina: white too, but with a black dot in the middle or a blue bar on top.
Long white with a blue-and-yellow strip on the left; Russia: fully white, no strip.
White with a blue strip on the left (green = agricultural). Croatia and N. Macedonia typically have no blue strip.
US/Canada: short plates, each state/province its own design. Europe: long plates with a blue strip.
